chief_complaint: intense left ear canal pain, itching, foul-smelling drainage, and exquisite pain when pulling on earlobe post-swimming (Otitis Externa)
hpi_details: 32F competitive swimmer presents with 3 days of severe left ear pain, intense ear canal itching, and a feeling that her ear is completely plugged with water and muffled. Yesterday started draining thin, yellowish, foul-smelling fluid onto her pillow. Pain is excruciating whenever she touches her outer ear, lies on her left side, or chews food.
ideas: thinks she trapped pool water inside her eardrum causing a middle ear infection
concerns: in severe sharp discomfort and unable to insert earplugs or sleep
expectations: wants antibiotic ear drops and clearing of the trapped water and debris

clinical_knowledge.topic: Acute Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Acute Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes aural toilet plus topical antibiotic-corticosteroid ear drops, avoiding ototoxic agents if the eardrum cannot be confirmed intact, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: intense left ear canal pain, itching, foul-smelling drainage, and exquisite pain when pulling on earlobe post-swimming (Otitis Externa)

Key HPI features: 32F competitive swimmer presents with 3 days of severe left ear pain, intense ear canal itching, and a feeling that her ear is completely plugged with water and muffled. Yesterday started draining thin, yellowish, foul-smelling fluid onto her pillow. Pain is excruciating whenever she touches her outer ear, lies on her left side, or chews food.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 74, Temp 36.8C. Inspection of left external ear shows erythema and crusting at the meatus. CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARK: Exquisite, jumping tenderness elicited by gentle traction/pulling upward on the pinna (auricle) or pressing inward on the tragus (this pinna/tragus tenderness distinguishes otitis externa from acute otitis media where pulling the earlobe is painless). Otoscopic examination after gentle suction micro-debridement reveals an intensely erythematous, edematous external auditory canal narrowed by 50%, filled with moist white/greenish debris and purulent exudate. Tympanic membrane is intact, mobile, and normal in appearance behind the canal swelling.
Relevant background/PMH: Swimmer's ear 2 years ago
Current medications: Over-the-counter drying drops (caused severe stinging)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Acute Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute otitis media (middle ear, different exam findings) without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Diabetes or immunocompromise with severe pain — raises concern for malignant otitis externa, a serious complication.
management_principles: Aural toilet: perform meticulous gentle suction micro-debridement under otoscopic guidance to remove purulent debris and ensure topical drops can physically reach the canal mucosa

Topical antibiotic-corticosteroid therapy: instil Ciprofloxacin 0.3% / Dexamethasone 0.1% ear drops (or Ofloxacin drops) 4 drops BID for 7 days; avoid ototoxic aminoglycoside drops (e.g. Neomycin-Polymyxin-Hydrocortisone) if the tympanic membrane is perforated or cannot be fully visualized
If the canal is severely swollen shut (>70% obstruction), insert an expanding Pope Ear Wick to mechanically draw drops down the canal, and keep the ear completely dry (no swimming x10 days)
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 32F swimmer presenting with acute otalgia, pruritus, otorrhea, and exquisite external auricle tenderness characteristic of Acute Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear).
reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 74, Temp 36.8C. Inspection of left external ear shows erythema and crusting at the meatus. CRITICAL DIAGNOSTIC HALLMARK: Exquisite, jumping tenderness elicited by gentle traction/pulling upward on the pinna (auricle) or pressing inward on the tragus (this pinna/tragus tenderness distinguishes otitis externa from acute otitis media where pulling the earlobe is painless). Otoscopic examination after gentle suction micro-debridement reveals an intensely erythematous, edematous external auditory canal narrowed by 50%, filled with moist white/greenish debris and purulent exudate. Tympanic membrane is intact, mobile, and normal in appearance behind the canal swelling.
reference_soap.assessment: Acute Otitis Externa (Swimmer's Ear) of the Left Ear, secondary to Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus proliferation in moist canal.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Aural toilet: perform meticulous gentle suction micro-debridement under otoscopic guidance to remove purulent debris and ensure topical drops can physically reach the canal mucosa. 2. Topical antibiotic-corticosteroid therapy: instil Ciprofloxacin 0.3% / Dexamethasone 0.1% ear drops (or Ofloxacin drops) 4 drops BID for 7 days. CRITICAL RULE: If the tympanic membrane is perforated or cannot be fully visualized due to swelling, strictly prescribe non-ototoxic fluoroquinolone drops (AVOID aminoglycoside drops like Neomycin-Polymyxin-Hydrocortisone which cause permanent sensorineural hearing loss if they cross into the middle/inner ear). 3. If canal is severely swollen shut (>70% obstruction), insert an expanding Pope Ear Wick to mechanically draw drops down the canal. Keep ear completely dry during bathing (no swimming x10 days).

learning_objectives: Differentiate Acute Otitis Externa (external auditory canal inflammation, exquisite pain on pinna traction or tragus pressure, normal or obscured eardrum, Pseudomonas/Staph etiology) from Acute Otitis Media (middle ear infection behind eardrum, NO pain on pinna traction, bulging erythematous tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks, Strep pneumoniae/Hib etiology)

Understand the absolute necessity of performing mechanical aural toilet/debridement and inserting an expandable cellulose Ear Wick when severe canal edema prevents topical drops from penetrating deeply

Select appropriate topical antimicrobial-steroid combinations (fluoroquinolone + dexamethasone) and recognize the strict contraindication against ototoxic aminoglycoside (Neomycin) preparations whenever eardrum perforation is suspected or confirmed
Outline water precautions and prophylactic acidifying ear drying drops (50% rubbing alcohol / 50% white vinegar) for frequent swimmers following recovery

teaching.one_liner: Bacterial infection of the outer ear canal from trapped moisture, causing severe pain worsened by touching the outer ear or pulling the earlobe, itching, and foul-smelling discharge — treated with topical drops, not oral antibiotics.
differentials: Acute otitis media (middle ear, different exam findings)
Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa in a diabetic
Contact dermatitis of the ear canal
red_flags: Diabetes or immunocompromise with severe pain — raises concern for malignant otitis externa, a serious complication

must_ask.say: Does it hurt a lot when you touch your outer ear or pull on your earlobe?
Is anything draining from your ear, and does it smell bad?
Does your ear itch, and does it feel plugged?

history.answer: My left ear has been hurting terribly and itching like crazy for the past three days.
It started three days ago in my left ear, and the pain and swelling have become steadily worse since then.
It's a severe, throbbing ache that jumps up to an eight out of ten, and it keeps me from sleeping at night.
Yes, pulling on my earlobe or pressing the little bump in front of my ear is excruciating, and even chewing food hurts.
It was intensely itchy deep inside the ear canal right before the severe pain took over, and it still feels itchy.
Yesterday morning I woke up with yellowish, thin, foul-smelling fluid stained on my pillow, but there was no blood.
My left ear feels completely plugged and muffled, exactly like water is trapped deep inside, and my hearing is dulled on that side.
No, I have not had any ringing in my ear or spinning dizziness.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, or sweats.
No, I haven't had a cough, sore throat, runny nose, or nasal congestion.
No, both sides of my face move normally, and I haven't noticed any blisters or rash in or around my ear.
No swelling or redness behind my ear, and I have not had any severe headache or neck stiffness.
I am a swim coach and competitive swimmer, so I am in the pool every day. When it started itching, I used cotton swabs to try to dry it out.
No trauma, no one hit my ear, and I haven't had any foreign objects or insects crawl inside.
No, I haven't been on an airplane or done any deep scuba diving recently.
My teeth don't hurt and my jaw feels fine normally, but chewing moves the ear canal and triggers intense pain.
No sore throat, no pain when I swallow, no voice changes, and no lumps in my neck.
I had swimmer's ear in this same ear about two years ago, but I have never had middle ear infections or a ruptured eardrum.
No, I have never had surgery on either ear.
No, I do not have diabetes and I have no immune system problems.
I think pool water got trapped behind my eardrum and caused a middle ear infection.
The pain is unbearable, and I cannot insert my earplugs, coach properly, or get any sleep.
I hope you can clear out the trapped water and debris and prescribe antibiotic drops to relieve the pain.
Other than the swimmer's ear two years ago, I have always been completely healthy.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I tried over-the-counter drying drops two days ago, but they caused terrible stinging so I stopped immediately. I take no regular prescriptions.
I do not have any allergies to medications, foods, or latex.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used vape products.
I only drink socially on rare occasions, maybe one glass of wine every few weeks.
I work full-time as a swim coach and competitive swimmer, and I live in an apartment with my partner.
There is no family history of hearing loss, ear disease, or chronic illnesses.
My last menstrual period started two weeks ago, my cycles are regular every twenty-eight days, and there is no chance I am pregnant.

exam.finding: Alert and in moderate distress from left ear discomfort, guarding her left ear, but sitting comfortably in no respiratory distress.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, heart rate 74 beats per minute, respiratory rate 14 breaths per minute, temperature 36.8°C, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air.

Left external meatus shows erythema and crusting; exquisite tenderness elicited by gentle traction on the left pinna or pressing on the tragus; no mastoid erythema or tenderness; otoscopy of the left ear shows external auditory canal narrowed by 50% with severe edema, moist white-green debris, and purulent exudate; tympanic membrane intact, translucent, and mobile; right ear canal and tympanic membrane are completely normal.

Whisper test reveals mild reduction in left ear; Weber test lateralizes to the left ear; Rinne test demonstrates bone conduction greater than air conduction on the left, consistent with conductive hearing loss from canal occlusion.
Facial nerve exam demonstrates full and symmetric forehead wrinkling, tight eye closure, and symmetric smile, with no focal cranial neuropathies.
Oral cavity, dentition, and posterior oropharynx are clear without inflammation; temporomandibular joints have smooth excursion without joint clicks or intrinsic joint tenderness.
No palpable preauricular, postauricular, or cervical lymphadenopathy; no neck masses or thyroid enlargement.
